conceptTag: Build on a platform you don't control
readerTitle: When your best sales channel belongs to someone else
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 베이커리와 배달 앱, 대형 유통사 내부 분석팀, 온라인 스토어 플러그인 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 남의 플랫폼 위에서는 매출보다 '고객 관계를 누가 갖는가'를 먼저 본다. 플랫폼은 빌려 쓰고, 고객과 퇴로는 내 것으로 만든다.
misconception: 플랫폼이 고객을 많이 데려다주면 그 고객은 내 고객이다. 같은 회사 안의 플랫폼이면 위험이 없다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨: BMO-07-03 게이트키퍼, BMO-07-06 플랫폼 리스크
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례(베이커리, 유통사 분석팀, 플러그인 회사)와 수치(주문의 약 40%가 배달 앱)는 가상입니다. 실제 배달 앱이나 스토어 플랫폼의 수수료·정책을 암시하지 않도록 이름과 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.
새 개념을 도입하지 않는 적용 레슨입니다. 4번 카드의 게이트키퍼·플랫폼 리스크 정의가 BMO-07-03, BMO-07-06 본문의 정의와 표현이 맞는지 게시 전에 대조하세요.

cards.title: When your best sales channel belongs to someone else
body: Maya's bakery gets about 4 in 10 orders through a delivery app. The app found her customers she could never have reached alone.
Then an email arrives. Next month, commission goes up. Shops that pay for a new *featured* program will rank higher in search. Nothing about her bread has changed. Her margins just did.

image.label: A baker reading a phone message beside a stack of delivery bags
image.brief: 작은 베이커리 카운터. 제빵사가 휴대폰 알림을 보며 굳은 표정. 옆에는 배달용 봉투가 쌓여 있음. 봉투와 앱 화면에 실제 배달 앱 로고나 색상은 쓰지 말 것. 따뜻한 일러스트 톤.

cards.title: What should Maya do first?
body: The app brings real volume. The new terms cut into what each order leaves her. She has a week to decide.

options.text: Leave the app in protest and focus on walk-in sales
options.feedback: She protects her margin but loses 4 in 10 orders overnight. The gatekeeper barely notices one shop leaving. Maya feels it every day.

options.text: Pay for the featured program to keep her ranking
options.feedback: Orders stay steady, but her platform risk grows. The app now knows she will pay more for the same customers.

options.text: Stay on the app, but start moving repeat customers to her own ordering channel
options.feedback: She keeps the reach while shrinking her exposure to one gatekeeper. It is slow, but each regular she moves is a customer whose terms she sets.

cards.title: Who owned the customer?
body: The app knew each customer's name, address, favorite order and how often they came back. Maya knew an order number and a pickup time.
Her regulars were, in practice, the app's regulars. The app chose who saw her shop, in what order, and at what price to her.
That is why a single email could change her business. She wasn't just selling through the app. She was **renting access to customers** on terms the owner could rewrite.

cards.title: Two ideas from this unit, working together
body: **Gatekeepers:** a gatekeeper stands between you and your customers and sets the terms of passing through. Ranking, fees and rules are its levers.
**Platform risk:** the more of your business runs through a platform you don't control, the more its decisions become your results.
Put them together and the question changes. Not *is this platform good for sales?* but *what happens to me when the gatekeeper changes the deal?*

image.label: A gate between a shop and its customers, with a toll sign
image.brief: 왼쪽에 작은 가게, 오른쪽에 손님들. 가운데 큰 문(게이트)이 있고 문지기가 'Fees', 'Ranking', 'Rules' 다이얼을 돌리고 있음. 가게에서 손님에게 가는 길이 문을 통과해야만 이어짐. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Three questions before you build on a platform
body: Ask these about any channel, marketplace or shared system your business depends on.
list: **How much runs through it?** The share of sales, leads or work that would stop if it changed tomorrow.
**What does it own?** Customer contact, data, pricing, ranking. Each one is a lever the gatekeeper can pull.
**What would leaving cost?** Weeks of work, or years of rebuilding?
cards.callout: High share, deep ownership, costly exit: that is where platform risk lives.
cards.softwareNote: App stores and online marketplaces work the same way for software. The store controls search ranking, fees and review rules, so an app with most of its users arriving through one store carries the same risk as Maya.

cards.title: Leaving isn't free either.
body: A second channel costs money and attention. Maya's own ordering page needs marketing, and many customers will keep using the app because it's easier for them.
Platforms often are the best deal available. They bring reach you can't buy any other way.
The goal isn't to avoid platforms. It's to know your exposure, keep some of the customer relationship in your own hands, and have an exit you could actually use.

cards.title: Your team runs on another team's system.
body: You lead the customer insights team at a large retailer. All your reports run on a data platform owned by central IT. IT plans a rebuild next year and says your team's custom tools "may not be supported."

options.text: Keep building as usual. It's the same company, so it will work out
options.feedback: Same company doesn't mean same priorities. IT is a gatekeeper with its own roadmap, and your platform risk is as real as Maya's.

options.text: Build your own separate data stack to stop depending on IT
options.feedback: It removes the dependency, but you take on cost, security work and duplicate effort. You may swap one risk for several.

options.text: Agree in writing what will be supported, and keep your core logic in a form you can move
options.feedback: You keep the shared platform's benefits while lowering your exit cost. You've turned an unknown gatekeeper decision into a known one.

cards.title: The platform builds what you sell.
body: Your small company sells a reviews plugin for a popular online store platform. Nearly all your customers find you in its plugin directory. The platform announces a basic built-in reviews feature, free for every store.

options.text: Ignore it. Your plugin is better than a basic version
options.feedback: Better may not matter if free is good enough for most stores. You are trusting the gatekeeper to keep leaving room for you.

options.text: Focus on needs the platform is unlikely to serve, and start supporting a second store platform
options.feedback: You move to ground the gatekeeper has less reason to take, and you cut platform risk by not depending on one directory for every customer.

options.text: Cut your price to match free as closely as you can
options.feedback: You may slow the loss of customers, but you shrink your margin while still fully exposed to the same platform.

cards.title: Rent the platform. Own the relationship.
body: This lesson used two ideas from the unit: **gatekeepers**, who set the terms between you and your customers, and **platform risk**, which grows with every share of your business you run through them.
**Try it today:** list your sales channels and the share of revenue from each. For the biggest one, write down what it controls and what leaving would cost.
